title: The effect of Relativistic Aberration on Cosmological Distances

candidates.claim_content: The paper defines the redshift as z := (λ_0 − λ)/λ, where λ is the wavelength measured in the rest frame of the emitting object (which recedes with speed ||v|| = cβ) and λ_0 is the wavelength measured by the observer, and then asserts that this equals sqrt((1+β)/(1−β)) (the longitudinal relativistic Doppler factor). Immediately afterwards (Eq. 5) the paper 'reverses' this relation to obtain β = ((1+z)^2 − 1)/((1+z)^2 + 1), and later (Eq. 12) uses sqrt(1−β^2)/(1−β) = 1+z.
candidates.suspected_defect: With z := (λ_0 − λ)/λ = λ_0/λ − 1, the longitudinal Doppler formula gives 1 + z = sqrt((1+β)/(1−β)), not z = sqrt((1+β)/(1−β)). As written, Eq. (4) is inconsistent with Eq. (5) and with Eq. (12) (ε = (1+z)ε'), both of which require the '1+z' version. The missing '1+' propagates into the definition of all the aberration factors.

candidates.claim_content: The paper defines the function appearing under the square root in the comoving-distance integral as H(z', Ω_M, Ω_Λ) := (1 + z'^2)(1 + Ω_M z') − z'Ω_Λ(2 + z'). This function is supposed to be exactly the quantity appearing one line earlier in Eq. (34), where the Friedmann equation is written as dt = dz / [H_0 (1 + z) sqrt((1 + z)^2 (1 + Ω_M z) − z(2 + z) Ω_Λ)], with Ω_M the matter density parameter and Ω_Λ the vacuum density parameter (Carroll, Press & Turner 1992).
candidates.suspected_defect: The first factor should be (1 + z')^2 = 1 + 2z' + z'^2, not (1 + z'^2). Eq. (36) therefore does not reproduce the expression in Eq. (34) from which it is supposed to be read off, and all subsequent integrals (Eqs. 35, 37, 39, 40) inherit the wrong integrand.

candidates.claim_content: The paper states the distance modulus relation m − M = 5 log_10(d_L/Mpc) + 25 (Eq. 25), where m is apparent magnitude, M absolute magnitude and d_L the luminosity distance in Mpc, and then inverts it in Eq. (45) to d_L = 10^{m−M−25}.
candidates.suspected_defect: Inverting m − M = 5 log_10(d_L/Mpc) + 25 gives d_L = 10^{(m−M−25)/5} Mpc. The exponent in Eq. (45) is missing the division by 5 (and the Mpc unit), so the stated inversion is numerically wrong by a factor 10^{4(m−M−25)/5}.

candidates.claim_content: In Section 2.3 the paper first defines the proper surface area dS_O of the cosmological object (CO) as seen in our reference frame by dS_O := r_O^2 dΩ_O, where dΩ_O is the solid angle subtended by the CO as seen by us and r_O is the 'observer area distance'. Later, in the same section, the paper writes 'let's correct equation 12 with the observed quantity as seen in our reference frame, instead that in the assistant reference frame, with the use of equation 26' and obtains dS_O = r_O^2 (1 + z)^2 dΩ_O (Eq. 28), from which it defines the angular distance d_A := r_O (1 + z) (Eq. 29).
candidates.suspected_defect: Eqs. (26) and (28) assert two different values for the same quantity dS_O (they differ by the factor (1+z)^2) with the same symbols r_O and dΩ_O; taken literally they are contradictory unless z = 0. Later (Eq. 43) the paper refers to 'a surface area dS'_O as defined in 28', suggesting the left-hand side of (28) should be a different (primed) quantity, but then r_O and dΩ_O on the right-hand side cannot be the same objects as in (26). The definitions of d_A and of the subsequent Etherington check depend on which version is used.

candidates.exact_quote:
this yields a natural definition for the angular distance

\( d_A := r_O (1 + z) \qquad (29) \)
candidates.claim_content: The paper argues at length that, because of relativistic aberration, 'the solid angle of the source dΩ_O in our reference frame is actually bigger than it would appear in a reference frame at rest with the CO', i.e. the observed solid angle is larger by a factor (1+z)^2 than the solid angle dS_O/r_O^2 that would be inferred without aberration (r_O is defined by dS_O := r_O^2 dΩ_O, Eq. 26, with dS_O the proper cross-sectional area of the CO). From this it writes dS_O = r_O^2 (1 + z)^2 dΩ_O (Eq. 28) and defines the angular distance d_A := r_O (1 + z) (Eq. 29), so that dΩ_O = dS_O / d_A^2.
candidates.suspected_defect: The factor appears with the wrong sign/direction. If the observed solid angle is (1+z)^2 LARGER than the aberration-free value dS_O/r_O^2, then dΩ_O = (1+z)^2 dS_O/r_O^2, i.e. dS_O = r_O^2 dΩ_O/(1+z)^2 and d_A = r_O/(1+z). Eq. (28) as written states dΩ_O = dS_O/[r_O^2(1+z)^2], i.e. a solid angle SMALLER by (1+z)^2, and Eq. (29) gives a LARGER angular distance, hence a smaller observed angular size — the opposite of the physical effect the section claims to be deriving.

candidates.exact_quote: Substituting equations 21 and 28 in it and using the definitions for luminosity distance 24 and for the angular distance 29 we immediately obtain the Etherington relation, which still holds
candidates.claim_content: The paper claims the Etherington relation d_L / [d_A (1+z)^2] = 1 (Eq. 31) follows from: (i) the photon-conservation identity dS_G dΩ_O = dS_O dΩ_G (1+z)^2 (Eq. 30); (ii) the definition dS_G = r_G^2 dΩ_G (Eq. 21), where dS_G is the telescope cross-section and dΩ_G the corresponding solid angle; (iii) dS_O = r_O^2 (1+z)^2 dΩ_O (Eq. 28), where dS_O is the CO's proper area and dΩ_O the observed solid angle; (iv) d_L := (1+z)^2 r_G (Eq. 24); (v) d_A := r_O (1+z) (Eq. 29).
candidates.suspected_defect: Substituting (21) and (28) into (30) gives r_G^2 dΩ_G dΩ_O = r_O^2 (1+z)^2 dΩ_O dΩ_G (1+z)^2, hence r_G = (1+z)^2 r_O. Then d_L/[d_A(1+z)^2] = (1+z)^2 r_G / [r_O(1+z)(1+z)^2] = r_G/[r_O(1+z)] = (1+z) ≠ 1. The Etherington relation only follows if one uses Eq. (26) (dS_O = r_O^2 dΩ_O, giving r_G = (1+z)r_O) instead of Eq. (28). So the claimed derivation is inconsistent with the equations it cites.

candidates.exact_quote: this doesn’t necessarily mean that the object is closer to us because the angular distance has a minimum, as stated in (Sandage 1961), in agreement with the correction of the luminosity distance 16 and 24.
candidates.claim_content: The paper's corrected angular distance is d_A = c/(H_0 sqrt(|Ω_k|)) · F( sqrt(|Ω_k|) ∫_0^z dz'/sqrt(H(z',Ω_M,Ω_Λ)) ) (Eq. 40), where F = sin, identity, sinh for closed, flat, open universes respectively and H(z') > 0 is the Friedmann function. The paper appeals to the existence of an extremum of the angular distance (equivalently a minimum of the observed angular size of a source of fixed proper size, θ = ℓ/d_A) to justify that high-redshift sources may appear larger.
candidates.suspected_defect: For a flat or open universe (F = identity or sinh) the right-hand side of Eq. (40) is a strictly increasing function of z, so the corrected d_A has no maximum and the observed angular size θ = ℓ/d_A decreases monotonically with z — there is no angular-size minimum in this model, unlike in the canonical case where d_A = R_0 r_1/(1+z) does turn over. The appeal to Sandage's turnover is therefore inconsistent with the paper's own Eq. (40), and it contradicts the section's claim that distant sources appear angularly larger.

candidates.claim_content: The paper asserts that the covariant velocity component of an object in a Riemannian spacetime with metric g_ik and coordinates x^i is v_i = dx_i/dτ = d(g_ik x^k)/dτ = (dg_ik/dτ) x^k + g_ik dx^k/dτ, and concludes from the first term that an object with fixed coordinates (dx^k/dτ = 0) can nevertheless have a nonzero observed velocity because the metric evolves.
candidates.suspected_defect: The step x_i = g_ik x^k is not valid in a curved manifold: the coordinates x^k are not the components of a vector, so index-lowering cannot be applied to them, and the covariant velocity is by definition v_i = g_ik v^k = g_ik dx^k/dτ, with no extra (dg_ik/dτ) x^k term. Hence the conclusion drawn from the first term (comoving objects acquire a nonzero velocity) does not follow from this manipulation; moreover in the FLRW metric g_00 = 1 and comoving observers have v^k = 0 for k = 1,2,3, giving v_i = 0 for spatial i.

candidates.exact_quote: As we can see, we have a decrease by a factor (1 + z)^−2 more than in the canonical treatment.
candidates.claim_content: The paper modifies Weinberg's derivation of the received power by multiplying the fraction of emitted photons intercepted by the telescope, πε^2/4π = πb^2/[4π R^2(t_0) r_1^2] (where b is the mirror radius, ε the angle it subtends at the source, r_1 the comoving coordinate of the source), by an extra factor (1+z)^{-2}, obtaining P = L [R^2(t_1)/R^2(t_0)] A /[4π R^2(t_0) r_1^2 (1+z)^2] (Eq. 14) and hence d_L = R^3(t_0) r_1 / R^2(t_1) = (1+z)^2 R(t_0) r_1, i.e. one factor (1+z) more than the canonical d_L = (1+z) R(t_0) r_1. The justification is that relativistic aberration makes the telescope subtend a smaller angle ε' = ε/(1+z) in the source frame.
candidates.suspected_defect: This appears to double count relativistic beaming. In the canonical result F = L/(4π d_L^2) with d_L = (1+z)^2 d_A, one already has F = L/[4π (1+z)^4 d_A^2], i.e. the full Doppler/beaming factor δ^4 = (1+z)^{-4} (two powers from photon energy and arrival rate, two from solid-angle/aberration via the Etherington relation). Moreover, the angle ε appearing in Weinberg's b ≈ R(t_0) r_1 ε is already the angle subtended at the source measured in the comoving (source) frame, so replacing it by ε' = ε/(1+z) inserts the aberration factor a second time.

candidates.exact_quote: from observations \(z_{CMB} \approx 1000\), so in this small angle approximation a small anisotropy will imply a solid angle \(10^{6}\) larger in our reference frame than in the assistant reference frame. The problem is that this effect happen for every point of the sky
candidates.claim_content: The paper claims that, because of relativistic aberration with (1+z)^2 ≈ 10^6 at z_CMB ≈ 1000, every patch of the CMB sky subtends a solid angle 10^6 times larger in our frame than in the frame comoving with the last-scattering surface, and that this happens 'for every point of the sky', producing a mixing/smoothing of CMB anisotropies with adjacent regions and thus an artificially more isotropic CMB.
candidates.suspected_defect: Relativistic aberration is a bijective (one-to-one, orientation-preserving) map of the celestial sphere onto itself; the total solid angle must remain 4π. It is mathematically impossible for all solid angle elements to be multiplied by the same factor 10^6 (this would require total solid angle 4π × 10^6). Aberration magnifies one hemisphere while demagnifying the other, and being a bijection it cannot 'mix' or blur distinct directions: the set of temperature values observed is simply remapped, so the amplitude of the anisotropies (and hence the claimed artificial homogenization) is not produced by aberration alone.

candidates.claim_content: The paper defines r_1(z, Ω_k, Ω_Λ, Ω_M) = F( sqrt(|Ω_k|) ∫_0^z dz'/sqrt(H(z',Ω_M,Ω_Λ)) ) with F(x) = sin x (closed), x (flat, Ω_k = 0), sinh x (open) (Eqs. 37–38). It then equates its own luminosity distance d_L = c(1+z)^2 r_1(z,Ω_k,Ω_Λ,Ω_M)/(H_0 sqrt(|Ω_k|)) with the canonical flat-universe one, written as d_L,can = c(1+z) r_1(z, 0, Ω_Λ,can, Ω_M,can)/H_0,can (Eq. 46), and divides to get Eq. (47).
candidates.suspected_defect: With Ω_k = 0 the definition (37)–(38) gives r_1(z,0,Ω_Λ,Ω_M) = sqrt(0) · ∫_0^z dz'/sqrt(H) = 0 identically, so the numerator of Eq. (47) vanishes and Eq. (47) yields H_0,can/H_0 = 0, contradicting Eq. (48) (ratio ≈ 1 at low z). The flat case requires taking the limit of the combination F(sqrt|Ω_k| X)/sqrt|Ω_k| → X; the right-hand side of Eq. (46) is written without the compensating 1/sqrt(|Ω_k|) that the left-hand side carries, so the two sides use inconsistent normalizations of r_1.

candidates.error_location: Section 3.3, final paragraph of the CMB discussion
candidates.exact_quote: while the temperature anisotropies of the CMB are in the order of \(10^{-6}\) K as measured in (Planck Collaboration et al., 2016)
candidates.claim_content: The paper states that the CMB temperature anisotropies measured by Planck are of order 10^{-6} K, and compares this numerically with the claimed solid-angle amplification factor (1+z_CMB)^2 ≈ 10^6.
candidates.suspected_defect: The measured CMB temperature anisotropies satisfy ΔT/T ~ 10^{-5} with T_0 = 2.725 K, giving ΔT ~ 3 × 10^{-5} K (rms of order 10^{-4} K including all scales), i.e. one to two orders of magnitude larger than the quoted 10^{-6} K. The numerical coincidence drawn with the factor 10^6 therefore does not hold.

candidates.exact_quote: if we are looking too far in the past, and this too far is extremely small as a new term \(\propto z^2\) is present in equation 39
candidates.claim_content: The paper's corrected luminosity distance is d_L = c(1+z)^2 F(...)/(H_0 sqrt|Ω_k|) (Eq. 39), while the canonical one carries a single factor (1+z): d_L,can = c(1+z) F(...)/(H_0 sqrt|Ω_k|). The text claims that the correction corresponds to 'a new term ∝ z^2' in Eq. (39).
candidates.suspected_defect: The new factor relative to the canonical expression is (1+z) = 1 + z, so the leading correction to d_L at small z is linear in z, not quadratic. The statement that the new term is ∝ z^2 (and hence that departures set in only at 'extremely small' look-back) does not follow from Eq. (39).

candidates.exact_quote: it means that the function \( F \) should decrease and/or that \( |\Omega_k| \) should be above 1
candidates.claim_content: Given d_L = c(1+z)^2 F( sqrt(|Ω_k|) X )/(H_0 sqrt(|Ω_k|)) with X = ∫_0^z dz'/sqrt(H(z',Ω_M,Ω_Λ)) and F = sin / identity / sinh, the paper argues that because the measured d_L is fixed while the prefactor acquires an extra factor (1+z), one must have F decreasing 'and/or |Ω_k| above 1'.
candidates.suspected_defect: Nothing in the equation singles out the value 1 for |Ω_k|: the requirement is only that the combination F(sqrt|Ω_k| X)/sqrt|Ω_k| be smaller than its canonical (flat, Ω_k = 0) value X, which is a statement about the sign of Ω_k (closed, F = sin, gives a smaller value for any |Ω_k| > 0) and about Ω_M, Ω_Λ — not that |Ω_k| > 1. Moreover for the open case (F = sinh) the combination sinh(sqrt|Ω_k| X)/sqrt|Ω_k| increases with |Ω_k|, so increasing |Ω_k| there has the opposite effect to the one claimed.

candidates.claim_content: In Eq. (43) the paper defines the observed specific intensity by I_ν dν := F_ν dν/dΩ_O = I_G 𝓘(ν(1+z)) dν/(1+z)^3, where F_ν is the observed flux per unit frequency given by Eq. (42) F_ν dν = F_G (1+z) 𝓘(ν(1+z)) dν / d_L^2, F_G := L/4π is the bolometric 'source flux' constant, 𝓘 is the normalized emission spectrum, d_L the luminosity distance and dS'_O the source surface area from Eq. (28); and it defines the surface brightness I_G := F_ν/dS'_O.
candidates.suspected_defect: The definition I_G := F_ν/dS'_O is inconsistent: F_ν is a frequency-dependent flux density, whereas for Eq. (43) to be a correct identity I_G must be the frequency-independent constant F_G/dS'_O = L/(4π dS'_O). As written, I_G depends on ν and the equation I_ν = I_G 𝓘(ν(1+z))/(1+z)^3 is dimensionally and functionally inconsistent with Eq. (42).
